meta.blurb: Samuel Smiles's famous book says that heaven helps those who help themselves. Meet the poor boys, patient workers and stubborn dreamers who built engines, railways and fine pottery, and learn what their lives can teach you.
meta.bible: Samuel Smiles: Scottish writer who published Self-Help in 1859; the book began as talks to young working men. Heaven helps those who help themselves: the old saying at the heart of the book. James Watt: Scottish instrument maker and engineer who improved the steam engine, a Condenser, with partner Matthew Boulton at Soho near Birmingham. Richard Arkwright: poor barber from Preston who made a spinning machine, the Water frame (patent 1769). George Stephenson: born 1781 near Newcastle, could not read until about eighteen, built the Rocket with his son Robert; the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830. Bernard Palissy: sixteenth-century French potter who burned his furniture and floors to feed his Kiln. Josiah Wedgwood: English potter of Staffordshire, built the works named Etruria; Queen Charlotte liked his cream-coloured ware. Isaac Newton: English scientist. Thomas Carlyle: Scottish historian; his French Revolution manuscript was burned by accident and he wrote it again. Michael Faraday: bookbinder's apprentice who became a great scientist; Humphry Davy was the chemist who hired him. Hugh Miller: Scottish stonemason who taught himself Geology. Thomas Telford: shepherd's son and stonemason who became a great builder of roads, bridges and canals. Walter Scott: Scottish writer whose printing business failed in 1826 and who worked to pay his debts. Horatio Nelson: British admiral. John Milton: English poet. Scotland. England. France. Glasgow. Greenock. Preston. Newcastle. Liverpool. Manchester. Staffordshire. Leeds. Voice and tone: practical, warm and encouraging, a series of true life stories each with one lesson; no invented facts.

B1B2: Samuel Smiles, a Scottish writer, gave talks to young working men who wanted a better life. In 1859 he turned those ideas into a book called Self-Help.
Smiles begins with an old saying: heaven helps those who help themselves. He believes that the best help for any person is the effort that person makes.
Smiles says that good laws are useful, but they cannot make a careless person wise. A person must decide to change, and that choice can only come from inside.
A nation is simply a large number of individual people. When each person becomes more honest and hard-working, the whole country becomes stronger.
Smiles knows that advice is easy to forget, so he tells true stories instead. He wants readers to see what real people did and then to copy their good habits.
James Watt worked as an instrument maker in Glasgow. One day he was asked to repair a small model of a steam engine, and it changed his life.
Watt's idea was to cool the steam in a separate part of the engine, called a condenser. It took him many years of testing, and he often had very little money.
A manufacturer named Matthew Boulton believed in Watt and joined him at Soho, near Birmingham. Together they built engines that soon pumped water from mines and powered mills.
Richard Arkwright came from a poor family in Preston, and he worked as a barber. In his spare time he became interested in a machine for spinning cotton thread.
Arkwright built a spinning machine driven by water, and he built large mills to use it. Some workers feared that machines would take their jobs, but he did not stop.
George Stephenson was born in 1781 near Newcastle, in a family with very little money. As a boy he watched cows and then took small jobs at a coal mine.
Stephenson could not read or write until he was about eighteen years old. He paid for lessons in the evening, after a hard day's work.
Stephenson learned about engines by taking them apart in his free time. He cleaned every piece and put it back, and soon he knew each part better than anyone.
Stephenson and his son Robert built a steam engine called the Rocket. In 1829 it won a famous contest at Rainhill, because it was faster and more reliable than the others.
In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, and Stephenson's engines pulled the trains. Soon railways were being built across the whole country.
Bernard Palissy was a poor French potter who saw a cup with a beautiful, shiny glaze. He did not know how it was made, but he decided to find out.
Palissy tried one experiment after another, and almost every one failed. When his wood ran out, he burned his own furniture and even parts of his floor to keep the fire hot.
At last the glaze came out smooth and bright, just as Palissy had dreamed. His beautiful dishes became famous, and people still admire them today.
Josiah Wedgwood came from a family of potters in Staffordshire. He left school when he was still a young boy and started to work at the potter's wheel.
Illness left Wedgwood with a bad leg, but he kept testing new clays and colours. He built a large works called Etruria, and Queen Charlotte liked his cream-coloured dishes.
Isaac Newton was once asked how he made his great discoveries. He is said to have replied that he had simply kept thinking about the same problem.
Smiles tells us that great things are made from small steps taken every day. A little work done again and again is stronger than one big effort.
Thomas Carlyle spent months writing the first part of a history of the French Revolution. A friend borrowed the pages, and a servant burned them by accident.
Carlyle felt very sad, but he did not give up. He started again from the beginning, and in time the book was finished and published.
Michael Faraday grew up in a poor London family. He worked for a bookbinder, and in his spare time he read the books that came into the shop.
A customer gave Faraday tickets to some lectures by the chemist Humphry Davy. Faraday wrote careful notes and sent them to Davy, who then offered him a job.
Hugh Miller worked as a stonemason in Scotland, cutting heavy blocks of stone all day long. When he split rocks, he often found the shapes of ancient fish and shells, and he began to study them.
Thomas Telford was the son of a poor shepherd in Scotland. He learned the trade of stonemason, studied hard, and later built many roads, bridges and canals.
Smiles says that people who succeed use their spare moments well. Ten minutes here and there may seem small, but over many years they add up to a great deal.
A strong will turns a wish into real action. Smiles says that people with energy often find a way, while those without it only find excuses.
Walter Scott was a famous Scottish writer, but his printing business failed in 1826. He owed a very large sum of money to many people.
Scott would not walk away from his debts, and he promised to pay back every penny. He wrote day after day, and his books paid back a very large part of the money, although the work wore him out.
Smiles says that courage is not only for battle. It also takes courage to refuse to do wrong when your friends are laughing at you.
Failure is never pleasant, but Smiles says it is a good teacher. We often learn more from our mistakes than from an easy success.
Smiles says that good habits matter more in business than brilliant ideas. The first and simplest habit is to arrive on time and to keep your promises.
Admiral Nelson is said to have told people that he owed his success to being early. He always arrived a quarter of an hour before the time.
A good worker pays close attention to small details and checks the numbers twice. Smiles says that small mistakes often grow into large ones.
Smiles says that honest dealing is good for business as well as for the soul. Customers return to a shop they trust, and workers stay with a fair manager.
Smiles says that people who plan their time get more done. A simple list or a regular routine can save hours of confusion every week.
Smiles says that money is a useful tool, but it should not become the goal of life. It should be earned honestly and used with good sense.
The most important rule about money is simple: spend a little less than you earn. Smiles believes that this habit makes a person free.
Smiles warns that debt can take away a person's freedom. Someone who spends money he does not have must always worry about the next payment.
Smiles believes in saving small amounts regularly, even when you have very little. Over many years the coins add up, and they can protect a family in hard times.
Smiles says that saving does not mean being selfish. A person should also be generous, and give to those in real need.
Smiles says that it is never too late to learn. A little study each day, even for a short time, can change what a person knows and what he can do.
The poet John Milton called a good book the precious life-blood of a great mind. Smiles agrees, and he says that books can be the best of friends.
Smiles says that we slowly become like the people we spend time with. For that reason we should choose our friends carefully.
Smiles tells us to look for good examples and to learn from them. When we watch a skilful, honest person, we pick up good habits without noticing.
Smiles says that a true gentleman is not made by money or by a famous family. He is known by his honesty, his good manners and his respect for others.
The message of Self-Help is clear: do not wait for others to rescue you. Start today, work hard, be honest, and take one step at a time.
C1C2: In the middle of the nineteenth century, a Scottish writer named Samuel Smiles spoke to groups of young working men who longed to improve their lives. He gathered the lessons of those talks into a book called Self-Help, which was published in 1859. It was soon read all over the world, and it has encouraged readers in many countries ever since.

The whole book rests on one very old saying, that heaven helps those who help themselves. Smiles argues that a person who waits to be rescued may wait for a very long time, while a person who works and plans steadily will find that doors begin to open. Nothing outside us, he insists, can do for us what our own effort can do.

Smiles admits that good laws and good governments are valuable, yet he refuses to believe that they can make a careless person thrifty or a lazy person industrious. A man who is helped too much, he warns, may in the end lose the habit of helping himself. Real improvement, in his view, begins in the heart and the habits of each individual.

A nation, Smiles reminds his readers, is nothing more than the sum of the men and women who live in it. If each of them grows a little more honest, a little more patient and a little more skilful, the whole country rises with them. No government, however wise, can do the same work from above, because it cannot reach inside each person's habits and choices.

Smiles distrusts advice that comes without proof, so he fills his pages with the true lives of men and women who rose against the odds. He believes that example is a quiet but powerful teacher, because we are far more likely to follow a person we can picture than a rule we have merely heard. Each story in the book, therefore, ends in a lesson that any reader can use.

James Watt, who had trained as an instrument maker and worked in Glasgow, was once asked to repair a small working model of an early steam engine. As he studied how it ran, he saw that the machine wasted an enormous amount of heat and fuel. Instead of simply mending it, he began to wonder whether it could be made much better.

Watt's answer was to cool the steam in a separate chamber, called a condenser, so that the main cylinder could stay hot. Turning that simple idea into a machine that really worked took him years of tests, disappointments and borrowed money. He was often close to giving up, but he always returned to his bench.

At last Watt found a partner in Matthew Boulton, a manufacturer at Soho, near Birmingham, who had the money, the workshop and the faith that the invention needed. Together they built engines that pumped water out of deep mines and turned the wheels of mills across the country. The poor instrument maker from Glasgow had helped to change the way the whole world made things.

Richard Arkwright grew up in a poor family in Preston and earned his living as a barber, shaving customers and making wigs. Yet his mind kept returning to the problem of spinning cotton, which in those days was slow work done by hand. Whenever his customers had gone for the day, he turned to his sketches and his small experiments, determined to find a better way.

Arkwright's water frame, which he patented in 1769, spun strong cotton thread far faster than any worker's hands could manage. He built great mills beside the rivers to drive it, even though some workers feared that machines would take away their jobs. His determination made him rich, and it helped to begin the age of the factory.

George Stephenson was born in 1781 in a poor household near Newcastle, where nearly every child was expected to earn a wage as soon as possible. He began by minding cows and doing odd jobs, and he soon found his way to the coal mines. Even then he was fascinated by the engines that pumped and hauled there, and he watched them whenever he could.

Stephenson could not read a single word until he was about eighteen, which troubled him deeply, for he sensed that knowledge was the key to everything he wanted. After long days at the mine he paid for evening lessons and practised his letters in whatever time was left. Slowly and patiently, he taught himself the skills that most children have learned long before they are ten years old.

Stephenson understood that reading alone would not make him a good engineer, so he spent his free hours taking engines apart to see how they worked. He cleaned each piece, studied its purpose and put the whole machine back together again. Before long, the men who had once laughed at him were asking him for help.

With the help of his son Robert, Stephenson designed a locomotive called the Rocket and entered it in a famous contest held at Rainhill in 1829. It ran faster and more reliably than any of its rivals, and the judges had little doubt about the winner. The poor boy who had once minded cows was now the most celebrated engine builder in the country.

In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway was opened, and Stephenson's locomotives carried passengers and goods between the two great cities. Within a few years, new lines were crossing the country, and travel that had once taken days could be done in hours. Smiles holds up the whole story as a lesson in what steady effort can achieve.

Bernard Palissy, a poor craftsman in sixteenth-century France, once saw a cup with a glaze so smooth and brilliant that he could think of nothing else. He had no money, no teacher and no real knowledge of the chemistry of glazes, which was still a mystery in those days. Nevertheless, in spite of all this, he made up his mind that he would discover the secret and make such pottery himself.

Year after year Palissy built his kilns, mixed his glazes and watched them fail, while his money disappeared and his neighbours called him mad. In the end, when he had no more wood to keep the fire hot, he is said to have burned his furniture and even the boards of his floor. Smiles shows this as an extreme case of a person who would not be beaten.

At long last, after so many ruined firings, the glaze came from the kiln smooth and bright, exactly as Palissy had imagined it. His dishes, decorated with fish, plants and small animals, became famous, and collectors still admire them today. The lesson Smiles draws is simple: success often waits for the person who refuses to quit.

Josiah Wedgwood was born into a family of potters in Staffordshire, and when his father died he left school at about nine years old to work at the wheel. He had little education, but he had a quick eye and a restless curiosity. Smiles notes that these two qualities, joined to hard work, were all that he needed.

An illness in childhood left Wedgwood with a painful leg, yet it never prevented him from testing new clays, glazes and shapes. He built a large new works, which he named Etruria, and his fine cream-coloured dishes pleased Queen Charlotte so much that they became fashionable across Europe. He had turned a small country trade into a fine art, and he had done it by patience and by careful, honest work.

Smiles reminds us that Isaac Newton, one of the greatest minds in history, was once asked how he had made his discoveries. His reply, according to the story, was that he had done it by keeping his mind fixed on the problem until the answer came. What looks like a flash of genius, then, is often the reward for long and patient attention.

Smiles argues that the greatest achievements are seldom the product of one dazzling effort; they are built, brick by brick, out of small acts repeated day after day. A student who works for an hour every evening will, in time, pass the clever friend who works only when the mood takes him. Steadiness, in other words, is a secret that talent alone cannot buy, and it is one that anyone is free to learn.

The Scottish writer Thomas Carlyle spent months on the first volume of his history of the French Revolution and then lent the only copy to a friend. A servant, mistaking the pages for waste paper, used them to light a fire, and months of labour went up in smoke. Carlyle, who had kept few notes, was left with nothing but his memory and his despair.

After the first shock, Carlyle took up his pen once more and began the whole volume again from the opening line. It was far harder to do the work a second time, but he did it, and the history was published to wide admiration. Smiles reminds us that real strength of purpose is shown not when things go well, but when we must start over.

Michael Faraday was the son of a poor blacksmith in London, and as a boy he took a job in a bookbinder's shop. He did not merely bind the books that passed through his hands; he read them, especially those on science, and tried out the experiments in a small corner of his own. Here, Smiles says, in a crowded little shop full of paper and leather, was the beginning of a great scientist.

A customer at the shop gave the young Faraday tickets to a series of lectures by the famous chemist Humphry Davy, and he listened with total attention. He copied out his notes neatly, bound them himself and sent them to Davy, who was so impressed that he later found a place for the young man as his assistant. From that humble start, Faraday rose to become one of the finest scientists of his age.

Hugh Miller earned his living as a stonemason in Scotland, and each time his hammer split a slab, it sometimes revealed the shapes of creatures that had lived millions of years before. Curious and patient, he borrowed books from friends, observed the rocks very carefully and taught himself geology. In time he became a respected writer on the subject, proof that the quarry can be as good a school as any university.

Thomas Telford was born to a shepherd's family in the Scottish hills, and he began life as an apprentice to a stonemason. He read widely, practised drawing and never missed a chance to learn from a more skilful man. By the end of his career he had designed roads, canals and bridges that were the pride of Britain.

Many of the people in these stories had no spare days, but each of them seized the spare minutes. A page read at the end of a shift, a problem turned over on a walk to work, a sketch made while dinner cooked: these fragments, Smiles points out, are more valuable than they look. Added together across the years, they separate those who merely wished to learn from those who actually did.

Smiles gives high praise to energy, which he describes as the power that drives a person from wishing to doing. A strong will does not remove the obstacles, but it makes a person look for a way over, under or around them, while a weaker character is content to stand and complain. In his view, the person who is determined to find a way will nearly always find one.

Sir Walter Scott was among the most popular writers of his day, but in 1826 the printing business in which he had a share collapsed. He found himself responsible for a vast debt, and many people expected him to settle with his creditors and begin a quieter life. Scott, however, was a man of a different mould, and he had no intention of leaving his name behind him in debt.

Scott refused to take the easy way out and promised instead to repay what he owed through his own labour. He wrote novel after novel at an astonishing pace, and the money from them cleared a very large part of his debt. The effort, sadly, wore down his health, but Smiles admires his honour as much as his industry.

Courage, Smiles insists, is not only the courage of the battlefield; there is another kind, quieter and often harder, which refuses to do wrong when everyone else is doing it. To say no to friends, to admit a mistake or to stand by an unpopular truth requires a firm character. Such moral strength, he suggests, is the best protection a person can have, and it is something that grows with every brave choice.

Smiles does not pretend that failure is pleasant, but he insists that it is among the best teachers we are ever given. The person who has stumbled and recovered knows things that the lucky person never learns, for mistakes teach patience, humility and the habit of trying a different way. Many of the great names in the book, he reminds us, were made by their failures rather than undone by them.

In his chapter on business, Smiles observes that success depends less on rare talent than on ordinary habits practised without fail. First among these is punctuality, which he describes as a kind of politeness and a form of honesty, since a person who is late steals the time of others. A reputation for keeping appointments, he says, is worth more than most people realise.

Smiles repeats a story that Admiral Nelson once said he owed his rise in life to being always a quarter of an hour before his time. Whether or not those were his exact words, the idea is a sound one, because a person who is early has time to think, to prepare and to stay calm. The extra minutes, it seems, can be more useful than extra talent, and they cost nothing at all except a little good planning.

Smiles stresses that a good worker is careful about small things, such as a column of figures, a letter or a promised delivery. Small mistakes, left alone, tend to grow into large ones, and a business that is careless in little matters will probably be careless in great ones. Accuracy may seem dull, but it is the foundation on which trust is built.

According to Smiles, honest dealing is not merely a moral duty but a sound business policy, for customers return to a shop they trust, and workers stay with an employer who treats them fairly. A fortune made by cheating is an unstable fortune, since it can vanish as soon as the truth is known. The wise merchant therefore builds his good name before he builds his wealth, knowing that the second depends upon the first.

Method, Smiles says, is the quiet partner of every successful person, for it allows a busy mind to spend its energy on work rather than on confusion. A simple list, a place for each tool and a regular hour for each duty will save more time over a year than any clever trick. Those who plan their days, he adds, are the ones who find they have time to spare.

On the subject of money, Smiles takes a balanced view: he neither worships it nor despises it, but regards it as a tool whose value depends on the hand that holds it. Wealth that is gained honestly and spent with good judgement can help a person and a family; wealth that becomes the only aim of life, however, usually brings little real happiness. The question, he says, is not how much we have but how well we use it.

The rule that Smiles repeats most often is also the simplest: spend a little less than you earn. A person who follows it will always have a small reserve to meet sickness, bad times and old age, while a person who ignores it will live on the edge of trouble, however large his income. This one habit, he writes, is the true foundation of independence, and it is within the reach of every person who earns anything at all.

Debt, according to Smiles, is a heavy chain, since a person who owes money cannot speak, act or choose entirely freely. He warns especially against living beyond one's means in order to impress the neighbours, which he regards as a foolish and expensive kind of pride. The habit of paying one's own way, on the other hand, brings a lightness of mind that no luxury can match.

Thrift, Smiles argues, is not a mean habit but a form of foresight, for small sums laid aside week after week can grow into a real protection against hardship. He also points out that saving is not the opposite of generosity: a person who has a little put by is the one best able to help a friend in need. Those who save carefully, in short, buy themselves both security for the future and the freedom to be kind to others.

Smiles is careful to separate thrift from meanness, for a person may save carefully and still give gladly where help is truly needed. The best kind of generosity, he suggests, is thoughtful rather than showy, helping others to stand on their own feet rather than leaving them dependent. In this way, he says, saving and giving become two sides of one honest and kindly character.

Smiles was convinced that learning has no age limit, and he gives many examples of men and women who began serious study late in life. A little reading and thinking each day, he says, adds up to a surprising amount of knowledge, much as small savings add up to a fortune. What matters, he says, is not where one starts or how old one is, but only that one begins and that one keeps going.

Smiles loves to quote the English poet John Milton, who called a good book the precious life-blood of a master spirit. A book, he says, allows an ordinary person to sit in the company of the wisest minds of every age, without leaving the fireside. It is a friend that is always available, never complains and never asks for anything in return.

We tend to become like the people with whom we spend our time, Smiles observes, for habits, opinions and even ways of speaking pass quietly from one friend to another. A person who keeps cheerful, hard-working and honest company is likely to grow in the same direction, while a person who prefers the careless crowd will be drawn the other way. The choice of friends, in short, is one of the most important choices we make.

Smiles holds that the best teacher is often a good example, for we pick up skills and habits from those we admire almost without noticing it. A young apprentice who watches a patient master at work learns more than any lecture could teach him. We should therefore look for people better than ourselves, and, when we find them, follow them.

At the end of the book, Smiles describes the true gentleman, who is known not by his fortune or his family name but by his honesty, his courtesy and his respect for himself and for others. Such a person may be rich or poor, and may work with his hands or his head, but he treats everyone with the same fairness. Character, Smiles concludes, is the finest result of all the efforts he has described.

The message of Self-Help, in the end, is a simple one: no one else can build your life for you, but you may build it yourself, one honest day at a time. Begin today, learn patiently, spend wisely, keep your word and choose your friends with care, and the effort will repay you in ways you cannot yet imagine. Smiles believes that the best help of all is the help you give yourself.
